In the spring of 1911 a young clerk named Emile Rouault arrived from Rennes and found work with a shipping firm that traded salt and cod with the Grand Banks. The office occupied the second floor of a stone house on the rue de Dinan, above a chandler's shop that smelled of tar and rope. Emile kept the ledgers, copied bills of lading and listened while captains blamed the weather for every late delivery. Most of the cargo went south along the coast, and a smaller share crossed the Channel on steamers that called at Portsmouth and Southampton. Coal arrived by rail from the mines near Fougeres, and the firm kept two small tugs for the heavier loads. The older clerks had seen the harbor at its worst. They remembered the winter of 1889, when a gale drove three colliers onto the rocks below the fort and the rescue boats came back empty. On the morning of the great storm the barometer fell all night, and by eight the sky over the city had turned the color of slate. The harbor master walked the quay with his coat buttoned against the wind and ordered the smaller boats into the inner basin. Emile watched from the office window as the first waves broke over the western mole and sent spray across the road. Around ten the rain arrived, hard and steady, and the fishing families gathered under the arches of the gate, waiting for news. Emile shared a room above a bakery on the place des Merciers, and on quiet evenings he walked the ramparts and watched the lights of the pilot boats. A boy ran up the rue de Dinan with a message for the chandler: the steamer from Jersey had lost an engine and would not reach the harbor before dark. The older clerks nodded, as if they had expected nothing else, and Emile copied the message into the day book, careful with his letters, while the wind pressed against the glass and the lamps swayed above the desks.
